title: The Mayo Brothers Build a Clinic
text:
William Worrall Mayo was an English-born doctor who settled in the small town of Rochester, Minnesota. His sons, William James and Charles Horace, grew up in his practice. As boys they rolled bandages, held lamps and helped at operations. Both studied medicine and came home to work with their father.

On 21 August 1883 a tornado tore through Rochester, killing dozens of people. There was no hospital, so the Mayos treated the injured in makeshift spaces, helped by the Sisters of Saint Francis. Afterward Mother Alfred Moes, the head of the order, proposed to build a hospital if Dr. Mayo would staff it. He thought the town too small, but she insisted. Saint Marys Hospital opened in 1889, with the Mayos as its doctors.

The brothers became famous surgeons. They worked as a team: while one operated at home, the other often traveled to learn new techniques from surgeons across America and Europe, then taught them to his brother. They invited other doctors to join them as partners and created one of the first group practices, in which specialists worked together on each patient.

In 1919 the brothers gave the bulk of their fortune to a nonprofit foundation, so that the clinic would serve patients and research rather than any family. They died within two months of each other in 1939. The Mayo Clinic still carries the family name.
lesson: A family's shared mission, and the willingness to share credit, can build something far larger than itself. Working as a team often starts at home.
people: William Worrall Mayo, William James Mayo, Charles Horace Mayo, Mother Alfred Moes
source: Helen Clapesattle, The Doctors Mayo (1941); Mayo Clinic historical records
